display_title: lacking in terms of novelty, clarity and experiments

content.title: lacking in terms of novelty, clarity and experiments
content.review:
This paper proposes a method for improving classification performance using similarity over multiple hierarchical levels. The basic idea is to introduce a loss at multiple levels in a deep neural network.

I think this paper is clearly not ready for ICLR. I will elaborate the details below.

Novelty
======
The novelty of this paper is very limited. The loss function in Eq(1-4) of this paper is heavily based on [Hsu & Kira(2015)]. From what I can tell, the difference with respect to [Hsu & Kira(2015)] is that the loss is applied on multiple levels in the neural network. I do not think such minor different is sufficient for an ICLR paper.

Also the idea of using hierarchical labels for fine-grained recognition has been explored in other papers as well (see below). This paper should compare with this work.

Yan et al.: HD-CNN: Hierarchical Deep Convolutional Neural Network for Large Scale Visual Recognition, ICCV 2015.

Clarity
=======
The writing of this paper should be significantly improved.

1) The paper actually never explains what "warm-start" is. And it never explains how Eq.(1-4) is used to improve the classification. This term "warm-start" only appears in the abstract and the conclusion. So it is very difficult to understand what the paper is doing. My guess is that it first learns a clustering based model using Eq.(1-4), then fine-tuned the obtained model for a classification task.

2) In Eq (2), both terms are loss(P,Q). What is the difference between them?

3) Figure 1 is never referenced in the paper. I am guessing Figure 1 probably corresponds to Eq(1-4), but the notations used in Figure 1 (e.g. L_1, L_2) never appeared anywhere in Eq(1-4). So it is very confusing.

Experiments
===========
The experiment is probably weakest part of the paper.

1) There is no comparison with any other hierarchical classification method.

2) This paper is built upon [Hsu & Kira(2015)]. Yet there is not even comparion wit [Hsu & Kira(2015)].

3) Table 1 is very confusing. First of all, there is no explanation on what "classification" in the table means. I am guessing this means directly training the a standard neural network classifier. If that is the case, it seems the warm-start classification proposed in the paper is not doing anything. For example, on the Birdsnap-34 dataset, it performs much worse than standard classification (50.32% vs 53.50%). Am I missing something here?

4) Looking at Table 2 and Table 3, it is also not clear what information they are conveying. Again, I assume "cross-entropy" means learning a standard classifier. If that is the case, it seems in most cases, "cross-entropy" performs as good as other alternatives in the tables. It does not seem the proposed method really offers anything.

Overall, it seems this paper is inconlusive. It is not clear to me that the proposed method actually boosts the classification performance.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Reproducibility Request
content.comment:
My group would like to reproduce your results as part of the ICLR 2018 Reproducibility Challenge (http://www.cs.mcgill.ca/~jpineau/ICLR2018-ReproducibilityChallenge.html). 

We want to reproduce your work on the birdsnap34 dataset by applying the same methodology.

Would you be able to provide the code you used for training and testing to help us reproduce your results with higher fidelity?

Thank you

content.title: Reproducibility Results (ICLR 2018 Reproducibility Challenge)
content.comment:
[ICLR 2018 Reproducibility Challenge (http://www.cs.mcgill.ca/~jpineau/ICLR2018-ReproducibilityChallenge.html)]

In the context of the Reproducibility Challenge, we tried to assess the reproducibility of this paper. In particular, we chose to focus on the reproducibility of one experiment method and the results. We not only used information available within the paper, but also information in the discussions on the OpenReview forum.

To assess the reproducibility, a divide and conquer approach was taken, by dividing the paper’s work into independent components and reproducing each individually while limiting the number of assumptions we hoped to be able to reproduce the results found by the paper. However, the main goal was to evaluate how reproducible the algorithms described in the paper were and whether the implementation could be achieved with reasonable effort.

First, we attempted to reproduce the datasets used in the experiments, particularly the less popular Birdsnap-34a dataset. Both datasets were easy to access, and we acquired the Birdsnap-34a subset of the Birdsnap-34 dataset for further investigation. Following the guidelines described in the appendix, we were able to reproduce the preprocessing steps by converting the images in YUV, computing the mean and standard deviation of the U and V channels before normalizing each image by its Y channel mean and standard deviation. While the paper states the mean deviation found for the R, G and B channels of the Birdsnap-34a dataset were, respectively, 0.485, 0.456 and 0.406, our reproduction calculated means of 0.482, 0.501 and 0.473.

Next, we tried reproducing the baseline classification results for the Birdsnap-34a subset using AlexNet; however, our efforts were inconclusive because there were an unreasonably high number of assumptions required to handle this less well known dataset. Random cropping and image resizing methods were among the assumed methods required to reproduce baseline results. Those assumptions and others direct us beyond the scope of reproducibility and into the realm of replicating a large portion of the experiment.

A main strength of the paper, in terms of reproducibility, is the usage of publicly available data for the two datasets used. In addition to this, information about the structure of the subset Birdsnap-34a was provided on the OpenReview website by the author enabling reproducibility of the data subset used in the experiments. While our normalization results diverge from the one stated in the paper, reproducing the preprocessing step was entirely doable based on the information provided in Appendix section A. Moreover, by presenting the mean and standard deviation of the images, preliminary comparisons of the datasets after acquiring them through a multi-step process are possible. These comparisons are meaningful for understanding differences in results that may occur as an artifact of data set differences rather than implementation problems.

The biggest challenge encountered during the reproducing process was the lack of code availability. Consequently, proper implementation of the methods applied to the Birdsnap-34 dataset was not achieved. The paper does not fully clarify the implementation used to achieve crucial components of the results such as resizing method applied to images of varying aspect ratios passed to a standard AlexNet. Finally, the computational infrastructure used to produce results was not mentioned. This created unnecessary uncertainty about computational resources required to achieve the same results as the ones claimed in the paper.

This paper does not promote efficient reproducibility. However, by adding a more descriptive explanation of the implementation, this can easily be overcome. Furthermore, providing the code used to obtain the reported results, regardless of how robust it is, the findings could be reproduced by a broader audience.

display_title: Needs revision, better experimental evidence and edits.

content.title: Needs revision, better experimental evidence and edits.
content.review:
This submission proposes to use hierarchical label information to impose additional losses on the intermediate representation in neural network training. 

Summary: 
The idea of the submission is clear, the execution not well done and the description of the method is lacking details. Form a technical perspective the proposition is not entirely novel, intermediate losses based on hierarchical information have been used before. The experimental part is weak, there is only an introspective view, and an experimental comparison with other approaches and more importantly on comprehensive benchmark datasets is missing, 


Details: 
The current state of the paper is not sufficient for publication. It is not technologically strong. More importantly the method may prove to be useful but the only experimental evidence for this comes from one single network on a constructed dataset (Birdsnap-34). The results on CIFAR10 using LeNet are largely un-informative and could be summarised more concisely. The submission closes with the parts that need be done in order to arrive at an informative and interesting contribution: comparison on compelling benchmarks (e.g., image-net using the synset hierarchy), comparison to strong baseline methods and more architectures. Will the reported finding using AlexNet on a single constructed dataset carry over to more realistic settings? If so, the paper can turn into an interesting observation. 

One obvious baseline is a random hierarchy for both datasets. Better results on manually constructed hierarchies would validate the point that it is the similarity that provides better regularisation. This is the main argument of the submission in the Introduction and this claim is not empirically validated.

More comments: 

- I disagree with the statement that “image classification in computer vision seems to do pretty well without using it (similarity)”. (Page1,paragraph2) I am not sure what this alludes to, visual similarity is the driving force behind computer vision classification. The similarity in the latent representations of higher levels in neural networks is strong enough to perform classification, what else if similarity between visually similar objects gives rise to good classification results? At least this statement is unclear. 
- “We have found that a value of two for the margin..” -> “We have found that a value of 2 for the margin..”
- Up to Section 2.1 it is unclear whether hierarchical information is needed or not. This is misleading, mainly because of the statements : contrastive loss does not require and explicit hierarchy; we only need weak labels for pairs of instances”. (Page 2,p2) and last sentence on page23: “only requires weak labels in the form of pairwise relationships.”. I understood this sentence that no hierarchy is needed. Later on, hierarchies are introduced (Section3 beginning explains how the hierarchies have been constructed for the datasets. ). So more than one pairwise label is needed between any pair of labels, depending on the level of the hierarchy. I suggest to formulate this better, this is a main part of the paper and the claims read stronger than they are.
- In Table 1 the Warm start classification is unclear. What exactly is the protocol for this experiment?
- I suggest to update the table or text to make clear that LeNet has only been used for CIFAR 10 and AlexNet for Birdsnap-34. (If this is the case, the sentence, “…extend their framework…” is ambiguous).
- Include all performance metrics (Clustering, NMI, Purity) for methods trained with Cross-Entropy
- The results on CIFAR10 are all very similar and pairwise tests are not included. Is this even a good object to study? I would suggest to remove this entirely and swap with a more challenging setup. I understand that this was probably the start point when developing the software but the results are not informative. 
- AlexNet D performing worse than AlexNet C seems to be a bug, Or is there another possible reason for this ?
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

display_title: Authors propose using a clustering based loss function at multiple levels of a deepnet as well as using hierarchical structure of the label space to train better representations.

content.title: Authors propose using a clustering based loss function at multiple levels of a deepnet as well as using hierarchical structure of the label space to train better representations.
content.review:
While I find the paper in it's current form useful and imformative there are a few places it can be improved. I would like to hear the thoughts from the author on the following points:

1. Using the loss function at multiple layers is already proposed before - ex: http://proceedings.mlr.press/v38/lee15a.pdf. While the motivation in this context is important authors should cite the previous work and talk about how it is different.
2. Compare AlexNet C performance to a state of the art residual net to really see if pre-training on ImageNet for higher capacity models still fall short to the proposed architecture.
3. Authors mention "We find that training with hierarchical labels results in the highest performance beating models with more parameters and approaches the performance of models pre-trained with ImageNet weights. This is a very significant finding since ImageNet contains multiple bird classes, so a model pre- trained with ImageNet has seen many more birds than a model pre-trained with pairwise constraints on Birdsnap34." - I am concerned about this conclusion on two fronts - we need to do the experiments on whole of birdsnap to make the experiment truly large scale and we also need to be careful in making assumptions of capacity of networks as pure capacity is not a good metric but rather state of the art architectures that use the capacity effectively is a good metric. For ex: As I mentioned before I would like to see a comparison with ResNet pre trained on ImageNet and AlexNet C rather than AlexNet double.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature
